etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English song, sang, from Old English sang, from Proto-West Germanic *sangu, from Proto-Germanic *sangwaz (“singing, song”), from Proto-Indo-European *sengʷʰ- (“to sing”). Cognate with Scots sang, song (“singing, song”), Saterland Frisian Song (“song”), West Frisian sang (“song”), Dutch zang (“song”), Low German sang (“song”), German Sang (“singing, song”), Swedish sång (“song”), Norwegian Bokmål sang (“song”), Norwegian Nynorsk song (“song”), Icelandic söngur (“song”), Ancient Greek ὀμφή (omphḗ, “voice, oracle”). More at sing.

definitions.definition: (music) A musical composition with lyrics for voice or voices, performed by singing.

quote.text: In the lightness of my heart I sang catches of songs as my horse gayly bore me along the well-remembered road.

definitions.definition: The act or art of singing.

quote.citation: 1884, Spencer Leigh Hughes, “The Weather. A Short Study on a Great Subject.”, in Golden Hours: A Monthly Magazine for Family and General Reading, volume XVII, London: Lile and Fawcett, […], page 28, column 1:
quote.text: How often the enthusiast has dwelt upon the birds bursting into song, the buds bursting into flower, all nature bursting into life!—as though a state of things in which everything around us is bursting is at all pleasant.

quote.citation: 1942, Robert Peter Tristram Coffin, The Substance that is Poetry (Patten Foundation series)‎[1], Macmillan, →LCCN, →OCLC, page 71:
quote.text: Or take one that is less of an explanation and more of a song , The Spider . I knew all along what I wanted to say about a spider . I wanted to say all the good things I could . For spiders are the one order of creation that I  thoroughly dislike. […]

definitions.definition: A melodious sound made by a bird, insect, whale or other animal.

quote.text: That most ethereal of all sounds, the song of crickets.

quote.citation: 1886, Peter Christen Asbjørnsen, translated by H.L. Brækstad, Folk and Fairy Tales, page 85:
quote.text: The robin alone by his soft morning song broke the silence and the solitude which reigned in the forest.

definitions.definition: (ornithology) The distinctive sound that a male bird utters to attract a mate or to protect his territory; contrasts with call; also, similar vocalisations made by female birds.
A low price, especially one under the expected value; chiefly in for a song.

quote.citation: 1810, Benjamin Silliman, A Journal of Travels in England, Holland and Scotland:
quote.text: his [a common soldier's] pay is a song.

quote.citation: 1913, Mrs. [Marie] Belloc Lowndes, chapter I, in The Lodger, London: Methuen, →OCLC; republished in Novels of Mystery: The Lodger; The Story of Ivy; What Really Happened, New York, N.Y.: Longmans, Green and Co., […], [1933], →OCLC, page 0016:
quote.text: Thus the red damask curtains which now shut out the fog-laden, drizzling atmosphere of the Marylebone Road, had cost a mere song, and yet they might have been warranted to last another thirty years. definitions.definition: An object of derision; a laughing stock.
